preamble: Lowering of the close back unrounded vowel [ɯ] to the close-mid [ɤ]. In Lungchow (Longzhou), a Central Tai variety, Proto-Tai *ɯː was lowered to /ɤ/ before alveolar codas: Pittayaporn (2009) states that PT *ɯːn and *ɯːl are reflected as /ɤn/ in Lungchow, while the vowel stays /ɯː/ in open syllables. In Tatar the Old Turkic high vowels became a reduced mid series (Johanson 1998, as summarized by Wikipedia): Proto-Turkic and Old Turkic *ï, a close back unrounded [ɯ] that contrasted with rounded *u, is Tatar ы [ɤ̆~ʌ̆], as in кыз [qɤ̆z] 'girl'. The same shift lowered *u to Tatar o (Proto-Turkic *kum > ком qom 'sand').

examples.note: Pittayaporn (2009) writes the high and mid back unrounded vowels as [ɯ] and [ɤ] where older sources use ï and ə (Lungchow fɤn for fən). Thai keeps /ɯː/ in these words: คืน /kʰɯːn˧/ 'night', อื่น /ʔɯːn˨˩/ 'other'.

Both vowels continue *ï. Proto-Turkic *ï contrasted with rounded *u, and Wikipedia gives its value as [ɯ]. The Tatar transcription [ʑɤˈlɤ] is from Wikipedia's Bashkir language article, which sets Tatar җылы against Bashkir йылы.

sources: Pittayaporn, P. (2009). The Phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University. https://hdl.handle.net/1813/13855
